design_detail: Prospective cohort within the Netherlands XTC Toxicity (NeXT) study (Brain 2008;131:2936-2945). 188 people who had never used ecstasy but were judged likely to start were imaged at baseline between 2002 and 2004, then followed with questionnaires. After a mean of about 17 months, imaging was repeated in 59 people who had begun using ecstasy and in 56 matched people who had not. Four imaging measures were compared: [123I]beta-CIT SPECT for serotonin transporter binding, proton MR spectroscopy for brain metabolites, diffusion tensor imaging for fractional anisotropy and apparent diffusion coefficient, and perfusion-weighted imaging for relative cerebral blood volume. Follow-up values were compared by linear regression adjusted for the baseline value, then for sex, baseline verbal IQ and follow-up age, education, alcohol, cannabis, amphetamine, cocaine and tobacco.
can_establish: That in people who had used on average 6 tablets (median 2) and were scanned a mean of about 19 weeks after their last tablet, serotonin transporter binding and brain metabolites did not change relative to people who did not start, while small differences appeared in diffusion measures in the thalamus and frontoparietal white matter and in blood volume in globus pallidus and putamen; and that the two groups did not differ on any imaging measure before anyone had used ecstasy.
cannot_establish: That heavier use leaves transporter binding unchanged (the doses here are very low and the tracer is insensitive, as the authors say); that the diffusion and perfusion differences are damage, are lasting, or are caused by MDMA rather than by the other drugs that rose more in this group; or that the absence of a transporter difference excludes a smaller one (no equivalence margin, intervals span the measured range).

sample.recruitment: Targeted site sampling, advertisement and snowball sampling in the Netherlands, 2002-2004, of people aged 18-35 who had never used ecstasy but intended to or had friends who used it (p. 2937).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Excluded: under 18 or over 35, past ecstasy use, severe physical or mental illness, psychotropic medication, pregnancy, intravenous drug use. Abstinence from psychoactive substances for at least 2 weeks and alcohol for 1 week before each session, checked by urine screen; nobody was excluded for a positive screen (p. 2937).
sample.demographics: At baseline 77 men and 111 women, mean age 21.7 (SD 3.0). At follow-up: 25 men and 34 women in the group that had started, 23 men and 33 women in the group that had not; age 23.0 and 23.1; Dutch adult reading test IQ 103.5 and 105.3 (Table 1, p. 2940).
sample.attrition: Of 188 at baseline, 158 (84%) returned follow-up drug questionnaires; 64 had started using ecstasy and 59 of these (92%) were re-imaged; 56 of the 94 who had not started were selected as matched comparisons. Not every person has complete data for every imaging method (Ns per method in Table 2, p. 2941).
sample.selection_effects: The cohort is self-selected by intention to start using ecstasy, so both groups are at higher risk than the general population; the comparison group was selected from the non-starters to match on sex, verbal IQ and cannabis use, which is a matched rather than random comparison; 30 people were lost before the follow-up questionnaires.

exposure.measurement: Validated Dutch drug-use questionnaires at baseline and follow-up, with four postal questionnaires in between; urine enzyme immunoassay for amphetamines, MDMA, opioids, cocaine, benzodiazepines, cannabis and alcohol before each session (pp. 2937-2938).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Cumulative use between baseline and follow-up: mean 6.0 tablets (SD 11.6), median 2, range given as 0.5-80 in the Results and 1-80 in the Discussion; 54% had taken one tablet or less and 17% ten or more; duration of use 20.4 (23.8) weeks; time since first tablet 39.2 (23.4) weeks (Table 1, p. 2940; Results, p. 2939; Discussion, p. 2943).
exposure.polysubstance: Between baseline and follow-up the group that started also increased alcohol (p=0.036), cannabis (p=0.029), amphetamine (p=0.047) and cocaine (p=0.017) relative to the comparison group; all effects of ecstasy remained significant after adjustment for these (Table 1, p. 2940; Results, p. 2939).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 2 weeks from psychoactive substances, verified by urine screen; mean time since last tablet 18.7 weeks (SD 17.5) (Table 1, p. 2940).

comparison.controls: 56 people from the same baseline cohort who did not start using ecstasy, individually matched on sex, age, verbal intelligence and cannabis use (p. 2937).
comparison.matching: Individual matching on sex, verbal IQ and cannabis use; the interval between sessions was shorter in the group that started (15.9 vs 18.3 months, p=0.024).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Almost none: this is the one design among the imaging studies with a pre-use measurement, and the groups did not differ on any imaging parameter, substance use or transporter genotype at baseline.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Comparison group also used alcohol, tobacco, cannabis and occasionally cocaine; their use rose less over follow-up (Table 1, p. 2940).

outcomes.instruments: [123I]beta-CIT SPECT 4 h after injection, specific-to-non-specific binding ratios in midbrain, thalamus and frontal, occipital and temporal grey matter, cerebellum as reference, with region-of-interest and voxel-by-voxel analyses; 1H-MRS (NAA/Cr, Cho/Cr, mI/Cr) in mid-frontal and mid-occipital grey matter and left frontoparietal white matter; diffusion tensor imaging (fractional anisotropy, apparent diffusion coefficient) in thalamus, putamen, globus pallidus, caudate and frontoparietal white matter; perfusion-weighted imaging (relative cerebral blood volume) in those regions plus four cortical regions (pp. 2938-2939).
outcomes.validity_norms: The SPECT tracer is not selective for the serotonin transporter and, as the authors note, animal work shows it underestimates MDMA-induced transporter loss; the striatal regions were not analysed because binding there is not serotonergic at 4 h. No normative values for any measure.
outcomes.operationalization: Neurotoxicity is operationalized as a change over follow-up in any of the four imaging measures relative to the comparison group.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None, deliberately: the authors state that they had a priori hypotheses and did not correct, to limit false negatives, while acknowledging the risk of false positives (p. 2943).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; image processing was largely automated (spatial normalization, segmentation, template regions).

analysis.effect_sizes: Serotonin transporter binding, regression coefficients for the group that started versus the comparison group, adjusted for baseline (Table 2, p. 2941): midbrain 0.036 (95% CI -0.068 to 0.140), thalamus -0.001 (-0.077 to 0.076), frontal grey matter -0.003 (-0.036 to 0.31 as printed), occipital -0.018 (-0.051 to 0.015), temporal -0.009 (-0.053 to 0.35 as printed); none significant, and the voxel-by-voxel analysis also found nothing. Brain metabolites: all nine comparisons non-significant. Significant differences: fractional anisotropy in thalamus -8.16 (-15.30 to -1.02) and frontoparietal white matter -8.23 (-14.35 to -2.10), both x1000; fractional anisotropy in globus pallidus +23.19 (3.65 to 42.73); apparent diffusion coefficient in thalamus +3.68 (0.67 to 6.69) x10-5 mm2/s; relative cerebral blood volume in globus pallidus -0.083 (-0.154 to -0.012) and putamen -0.058 (-0.110 to -0.006). Percentage changes were under 5%. No dose-response relation with cumulative tablets within the group that started.
analysis.covariates: Model 1 adjusted for the baseline value; model 2 added sex, baseline verbal IQ, follow-up age, years of education and use of alcohol, cannabis, amphetamines, cocaine and tobacco; all significant effects persisted (p. 2939).
analysis.preregistration_detail: A design paper for the NeXT study was published in 2005 (de Win et al., Int J Methods Psychiatr Res 14:167-185) and is cited for methods, but no trial-registry record or pre-specified analysis plan is cited; the design paper was not read here.
analysis.selective_reporting: All 32 region-by-measure comparisons are tabulated with intervals, including the many null results.
analysis.power: Not formally calculated; the authors state that power may have been insufficient for SPECT and spectroscopy given the very low doses, and that the SPECT tracer may be too insensitive (p. 2943).

interpretation_gap.results_show: After people had taken a median of 2 ecstasy tablets, serotonin transporter binding and brain metabolites were unchanged relative to matched people who did not start, while four small differences appeared in diffusion and perfusion measures, each under 5% and within the normal range for the age group, with no relation to the number of tablets taken.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title speaks of 'sustained effects of ecstasy on the human brain' and the abstract concludes that the findings suggest effects on brain microvasculature, white-matter maturation and possibly axonal damage, and that neurotoxicity of even low doses cannot be excluded (abstract, p. 2936). The Discussion concedes that the study offers no undisputable evidence of causality, that no dose-response was found, that confounding by other substances cannot be fully excluded, that no correction for multiple comparisons was applied, and that the changes may be reversible adaptations (pp. 2943-2944). The headline claim therefore rests on 6 of 32 comparisons, uncorrected, in the absence of the transporter change the study was designed to detect.

replication.where_it_stands: No second prospective imaging cohort of people starting to use ecstasy has been published; this remains the only study with pre-use brain measurements, and its transporter null is routinely read as showing that very low doses do not produce a detectable transporter change rather than that no change occurs.

funding.funder: Netherlands Organization for Health Research and Development (ZonMw 310-00-036); a BSIK grant from the Dutch Ministry of Education, Culture and Science for one author's informatics work (Funding, p. 2944).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement appears in the article (searched in the text extraction of all pages).
funding.affiliations_note: Academic Medical Center Amsterdam and Utrecht; the same group published the Lancet SPECT study of 2001 (Reneman et al.), whose authors are co-authors here.

what_would_settle_it: The same prospective design with a selective PET tracer rather than [123I]beta-CIT, in people who go on to heavier use, with repeated scanning over years and pre-specified outcomes, so that a transporter change and its reversal could be observed in the same people.

domains.note: Baseline imaging, substance use and genotype did not differ, which removes most premorbid confounding; but use of alcohol, cannabis, amphetamine and cocaine rose more in the group that started, and the adjustment for these is by self-report.
Self-reported tablets with urine screens at sessions only; tablet content unverified, though the authors cite national monitoring that over 95% of Dutch tablets contained MDMA.

People selected for intending to start using ecstasy; 30 of 188 lost before follow-up questionnaires and 5 of 64 starters not re-imaged; the comparison group was selected by matching from the non-starters.
Complete data were not available for every method in every person (for example SPECT in 53 and 57 of the two groups), and the reasons are described only as technical problems or refusal.

The SPECT tracer is not selective for the serotonin transporter and is described by the authors as probably too insensitive for small changes; the diffusion and perfusion measures are non-specific; no blinding of processing is reported.
All comparisons are tabulated, which is good practice, but 32 tests were run without correction and the title and abstract are built on the 6 that reached p<0.05.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The design is the strongest available for this question, and the pre-use equivalence of the groups is a real strength; the weaknesses are the insensitive transporter tracer, very low doses, uncorrected multiplicity and a headline built on small differences in non-specific measures. It can be cited for the absence of a detectable transporter change after a median of 2 tablets and for the baseline equivalence of the groups, not for the presence of neurotoxicity.

key_findings.finding: Serotonin transporter binding did not differ at follow-up in any region: midbrain 0.036 (95% CI -0.068 to 0.140), thalamus -0.001 (-0.077 to 0.076), frontal -0.003 (-0.036 to 0.31 as printed), occipital -0.018 (-0.051 to 0.015), temporal -0.009 (-0.053 to 0.35 as printed); the voxel-by-voxel analysis also showed no effect.
key_findings.note: The upper limits for frontal (0.31) and temporal grey matter (0.35) are printed as such in Table 2 and checked on the rendered page; given the coefficients and lower limits they are almost certainly misprints for 0.031 and 0.035 (see reporting issues). The occipital and frontal binding ratios are close to zero in both groups (0.03 to 0.06), so percentage differences computed from them, as later reviews do, are not meaningful.

key_findings.finding: Brain metabolite ratios (NAA/Cr, Cho/Cr, mI/Cr in three voxels) showed no effect of starting to use ecstasy.

Fractional anisotropy fell in the thalamus (-8.16, 95% CI -15.30 to -1.02, x1000) and frontoparietal white matter (-8.23, -14.35 to -2.10) and rose in the globus pallidus (+23.19, 3.65 to 42.73); the apparent diffusion coefficient rose in the thalamus (+3.68, 0.67 to 6.69); relative cerebral blood volume fell in the globus pallidus (-0.083, -0.154 to -0.012) and putamen (-0.058, -0.110 to -0.006).
key_findings.note: All changes were under 5% and, as the paper says, within the normal range of the age group; part of each difference comes from an increase in the comparison group over follow-up.

key_findings.finding: The two groups did not differ on any imaging parameter, on substance use or on serotonin-transporter genotype at baseline, before anyone had used ecstasy.
key_findings.locator: Results, 'Characteristics of the sample and substance use' (p. 2939); Table 2, baseline columns (p. 2941)

key_findings.finding: Cumulative use was a mean of 6.0 tablets (SD 11.6), median 2; 54% had taken one tablet or less and 17% ten or more; mean time since the last tablet was 18.7 weeks (SD 17.5).
Within the group that started, there was no relation between cumulative tablets and any follow-up imaging measure.
All significant effects persisted after adjustment for sex, baseline verbal IQ, age, education and use of alcohol, cannabis, amphetamines, cocaine and tobacco.

reporting_issues.issue: The Introduction says the 59 people who started were compared with 58 people who remained ecstasy-naive, while the abstract, Methods and Table 1 give 56.
reporting_issues.consequence: Internal inconsistency in the sample size of the comparison group; the tabulated analyses use 56 (and fewer for individual imaging methods).

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2 the upper confidence limits for transporter binding in frontal grey matter (0.31) and temporal grey matter (0.35) are printed with one digit too few for their own rows: the coefficients are -0.003 and -0.009 with lower limits -0.036 and -0.053, and every other interval in the table is symmetrical about its coefficient.
reporting_issues.consequence: Read as printed, the frontal interval would span -0.036 to 0.31 on a measure whose group means are 0.00 and 0.01, which is not credible; the intended values are almost certainly 0.031 and 0.035. Checked on the rendered page, where the figures read 0.31 and 0.35. Anyone quoting these intervals should say which reading they use.

reporting_issues.issue: The cumulative dose range is given as 0.5-80 tablets in the Results and as 1-80 in the Discussion.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the median of 2 tablets is the figure that matters for interpretation.

reporting_issues.issue: No correction for multiple comparisons was applied to 32 region-by-measure tests, by explicit choice.
reporting_issues.consequence: With 32 tests, one or two results at p<0.05 would be expected by chance; six were found, four of them in the same two measures, so the pattern is not purely chance, but individual findings (for example the increase in pallidal anisotropy) are fragile.

reporting_issues.issue: The interval between the two sessions was shorter in the group that started than in the comparison group (15.9 vs 18.3 months, p=0.024), and several of the significant differences arise partly from increases in the comparison group over that interval.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper itself reads the white-matter difference as failure of normal maturation in the group that started; a difference in follow-up time between groups works in the same direction and is not adjusted for.

reporting_issues.issue: The title and abstract present 'sustained effects on the human brain' and possible axonal damage although the study's primary serotonergic measures were null and no dose-response was found.
reporting_issues.consequence: The conclusion that is most often quoted from this paper is weaker than it appears; the Discussion's own caveats are not carried into the abstract.
